blocks.html:
Motion skills: where to extract the techniques

Video creation studies · Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A skill is a prompt with taste. Our skill trial found that no third-party skill beat a control built with none, and that every skill collided with the owner's rules at least once. What is worth taking is a single technique together with its evidence, and this page lists where each technique can be taken from.

Licences below were checked on the dates in the trial; they can change, so check the repository before copying anything. Verdicts are from the October 19, 2026 trial: one 39 s story, one run per skill, one auditor.

Rules for taking from a skill

  • Install nothing. An installed skill can change defaults silently, and copying files brings in licence terms. Keep the repositories as reading.
  • Read as data, run no code. Never run an installer or a script from a skill you have not reviewed.
  • Check the licence. AGPL and "none stated" mean reading only.
  • List conflicts first. Each skill in the trial collided with an owner rule: a moving camera, camera travel, region highlights, never-ship items.
  • Build a control. Make the same scene without the skill and let an independent check rank them by the owner's rules.
  • A checklist that demands change needs a fact to show. One checklist item pushed a builder to invent a meaning on a map; the change must use facts already in the fact table.

Skills released after October 19, 2026 and the roughly 34 downloaded repositories that were not applied have not been evaluated.

Motion techniques Claude can use

Video creation studies · Reviewed November 16, 2026

This is the practical side of the studies: each technique the tutorials describe, pulled out as its own article with a small animated demo, so an assistant (or a person) can apply it one at a time. The main source is ProdAdvice's HyperFrames tutorial (K1Mr5_7Gm3g); we add the two other tutorials the owner picked, Studio Igor's game-art experiments (YQ01D9xGAnk) and Andrey Zenin's 2D video plugin tutorial (YyUP_hSovOg). The second wave of techniques comes from a fourth tutorial found in the chat history, ИИ МАСТОДОНТ's "Sonnet 5.5 and HyperFrames" (yEpN_s9UkAE), and from the prompts in this site's own Videos catalog, mainly the detailed ones by flxrnc, techhalla and 0xnicc0 (their authors' X posts are linked in each article). The third wave comes from the owner's curves project (harmonic shapes, letters and sound, accumulated clocks) and from 3D work: our Tabletop Miniature style and a small Blender test we ran. We read the transcript and the prompts; we have not rerun them.

How to use them

  1. Start from the workflow group: a timing plan and a style contract cost minutes and prevent most rework.
  2. Pick one look technique for the job and test it on one short scene. Do not stack all four of the pencil techniques on a first attempt.
  3. Run render and inspect on every scene, and keep the error log current.
  4. For narrated pieces add the picture-and-voice group.
  5. For product and UI motion, or pieces that loop or go to music, add the motion-engineering group (seekable frame first) and the direction-and-review group.
  6. For character and shape work add the harmonic group; for 3D scenes, the 3D group (the Blender article is a measured test, the others come from a finished style).

Limits

The demos are our own drawings that show how each mechanism works. They are not frames from the tutorials, and the numbers inside them (amplitudes, spacings, pixel shifts) are illustrative unless an article says a number comes from a source. The code snippets are our proposed implementations; none of the four tutorials publishes its source, and the prompts in the catalog are given without their code. A technique that works in a demo has to be tested on a real scene, with the checks in Auditing a video, before it enters a client video.

title: Technique: build long work from short approved pieces
label: Short pieces
summary: Make and approve one short scene at a time, then join them and review only the seams.

blocks.html:
Technique: build long work from short approved pieces

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The creator says outright that long pieces are easier to build as smaller sections (10:14). The tutorial on a code-drawn 2D video plugin shows the same habit from another angle: it renders a pilot of about 30 s before the full video, and the author then picks one scene of the pilot to change (6:39).

blocks.caption: Four scenes of 5 s, each approved on its own, slide together into one 20 s strip. The three seams get a review flag for palette, audio and pacing.

blocks.html:
How it works

  1. Split the story into scenes of a few seconds, each with one idea. The demo uses four scenes of 5 s.
  2. Build and approve each scene alone against the style contract, with its own render and inspect pass. A defect is found in 5 s of film, not in 20.
  3. Join them into one timeline. The scenes share the palette, the seed rules and the audio bed.
  4. Review the seams. With four scenes there are three. Look at the last frame of one and the first of the next, and listen for a jump in level or ambience.

Why it helps

  • A correction touches one scene, so the others are not at risk.
  • Scenes are reusable: an approved opening can be placed in the next film.
  • A pilot gives early feedback. Render the first 8 to 10 s at draft quality and show it before the full build; after a render, send the owner a numbered sheet with one thumbnail per shot, so feedback can name a shot (see Reference: 2D video plugin).

Watch for

  • Seams. Matching colour, grain and sound level at the cut is the work that remains. A shared contract prevents most of it; the review catches the rest.
  • Scenes that cannot stand alone. If scene 3 needs scene 2 to make sense, approve them as a pair.
  • Per-scene seeds that reuse the same drawing. Two scenes with one seed will boil in lockstep. See Drawing cadence and a stable seed.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 10:14-11:41; Andrey Zenin, YyUP_hSovOg at 6:39-7:25. The 4 x 5 s split is our illustration.

title: Technique: a beat grid
label: Beat grid
summary: Put every move, click and sound on a fixed grid of beats so a piece without a soundtrack still feels in time, and music can be added later.

blocks.html:
Technique: a beat grid

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Prompts for product motion often start from a grid of time, not from a list of effects. One gives a 0.5 s beat grid and lists what happens at each beat, from "0.0 pixel mascot idles" to "12.0 toast shrinks back into the mascot" (flxrnc). Another sets 120 BPM and says something must land on every beat for the first 16 beats, and after that on every other beat (techhalla). A third wants 24 beats at 120 BPM "and something happens on every beat" (0xnicc0); a fourth syncs everything to a 128 BPM grid (BuildFastWithAI).

blocks.caption: A 4 s axis at 120 BPM: a heavy tick every 0.5 s, a light tick every 125 ms. Six events sit on beats. A hit that started at 1.3 s slides to the beat at 1.5 s.

blocks.html:
How it works

At 120 BPM one beat is 0.5 s and a sixteenth note is 125 ms. If every entrance, click and impact is placed on that grid, the piece has a pulse before any sound exists, and a track at the same tempo fits with no re-timing. The 125 ms step also gives a natural stagger for letters.

How to build it

Put the grid in the timing plan and snap to it:

const BPM = 120, beat = 60 / BPM;            // 0.5 s
const onGrid = (t) => Math.round(t / beat) * beat;
const plan = { mascotSquash: onGrid(1.0), loader: onGrid(1.5), check: onGrid(2.0) };

With real music, find the track's own grid first: start on a downbeat and place each click and chime on a measured peak (0xnicc0 asks for exactly this, with a royalty-free track near 120 BPM).

Watch for

  • Every beat filled for ever. The prompt that fills the first 16 beats relaxes to every other beat afterwards. Constant hits tire the eye.
  • A grid that fights the story. Sentences have their own timing; see one sentence, one shot. Use the grid for UI and motion pieces, voice timing for narrated ones.
  • Rounding the tempo. A track at 118 BPM on a 120 BPM grid drifts out in a few bars.

Sources: flxrnc-251921, techhalla-498547, 0xnicc0-516612, BuildFastWithAI in our prompt database; the onGrid snippet is ours.

title: Technique: a Blender animation as frame numbers
label: Blender frames
summary: Script Blender without its interface, key a scene, and render every frame from its number. We ran a small test and measured what comes out.

blocks.html:
Technique: a Blender animation as frame numbers

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Blender can sit in this workflow the way Three.js does: a 3D element made by a script, with a motion that is a function of the frame number, rendered to still images and laid into the video. Nothing in this collection covered Blender, so we ran a small test ourselves. It covers only what we measured, and the limits are listed below.

blocks.caption: The four steps of the test, and the cube position at five frames. Orange line: the default Bezier interpolation. Dashed: linear. The numbers are what the script printed.

blocks.html:
What we ran

Blender 5.2.2 LTS, headless, with this script (/Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender -b -P test.py):

import bpy
sc = bpy.context.scene
sc.frame_start, sc.frame_end = 1, 48
sc.render.engine = "BLENDER_WORKBENCH"
sc.render.resolution_x, sc.render.resolution_y = 320, 180
cube = bpy.context.object
cube.location.x = -2; cube.keyframe_insert("location", index=0, frame=1)
cube.location.x =  2; cube.keyframe_insert("location", index=0, frame=48)

act, slot = cube.animation_data.action, cube.animation_data.action_slot
fc = next(f for f in act.layers[0].strips[0].channelbag(slot).fcurves
          if f.data_path == "location" and f.array_index == 0)
print([round(fc.evaluate(f), 3) for f in (1, 12, 24, 36, 48)])
sc.frame_set(24)                      # the scene is now exactly frame 24
sc.render.filepath = "out/"; bpy.ops.render.render(animation=True)

What we measured

  • The value is a function of the frame. With the default Bezier keys, fc.evaluate gave -2, -1.445, -0.064, 1.351 and 2 at frames 1, 12, 24, 36, 48. After frame_set(5) and then frame_set(24) the cube was at the same x as before.
  • Default is not linear. The Bezier join eases in and out: at frame 12 the cube is at -1.445, where a linear join gives -1.064. For a steady travel set the keys to LINEAR.
  • Same frame, same file. Frame 24 rendered twice gave identical PNG files.
  • Fast enough to iterate. 48 frames in Workbench at 320 by 180 took 0.4 seconds. This says nothing about Eevee or Cycles at full size.
  • The curves API moved. In 5.2.2 action.fcurves was not there. Curves live on a channel bag: action.layers[0].strips[0].channelbag(slot).fcurves. Older recipes you find online break on it.

This is the same contract as a seekable frame: render frame n from n alone. Keys placed on Bezier handles can be shaped like the camera curves; for a rig, key the camera object the same way.

How it fits a video

Render the 3D part as a numbered PNG sequence (a transparent background is a render setting; we did not test it) and treat it as a layer: lay it over the 2D scene, mask it, and check it frame by frame as in render and inspect. Use Blender when the object needs modelling, materials or physically based light. Use Three.js, as in the camera curves article, when the whole scene is real-time and shares the page clock.

Not tested

Encoding to a video file, a transparent background, Eevee and Cycles, GPU rendering, rigs, simulations, and a long sequence. The Blender add-on for live control was not connected in this session, so the test used the command line only.

Sources: our own run, as above; Blender Python API for the names used. The installed Blender skill documents the same area.

title: Technique: drawing cadence and a stable seed
label: Cadence and seed
summary: Why the redraw rhythm must come from time, not from the frame number, and why the random numbers must be seeded so a re-render gives the same picture.

blocks.html:
Technique: drawing cadence and a stable seed

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Line boil needs two decisions that look like details and decide whether the effect survives a render. First, how often a new drawing appears, independent of the video's frame rate. Second, which random numbers a given moment uses, so that the same moment always looks the same.

Cadence is not the frame rate

ProdAdvice contrasts 24 and 12 fps with a ball example (08:22). The part that carries over to a production file is the idea, not the setting: the drawing rate is a look, and the file rate is a delivery format.

blocks.caption: Half a second at 12 drawings a second. The drawing rhythm stays the same; only the number of frames each drawing holds changes with the file rate.

blocks.html:
The drawing index is floor(time * 12). In a 24 fps file each drawing holds 2 frames. In a 30 fps file the holds alternate between 3 and 2 frames. Both show the same six drawings in half a second.

A seed makes a moment repeatable

A renderer may visit the same time more than once: it seeks, it re-renders a failed chunk, you scrub back to check a defect. If the outline uses a random number at every call, the second visit draws a different contour, and the defect you saw is gone or a new one appears.

blocks.caption: The same three visits to the timeline: 0.5 s, 1.0 s, then 0.5 s again. With a random number the third circle differs from the first; with a seed that comes from the scene seed plus the drawing index it is identical.

blocks.html:
The fix is one line: seed the generator with the scene seed plus the drawing index, seed = sceneSeed + floor(time * 12). Then 0.5 s is drawing 6 every time, and 1.0 s is drawing 12.

Checklist

  1. Compute the drawing index from time, never from a frame counter.
  2. Give each scene one fixed seed and store it with the scene, so a revision does not reshuffle every line.
  3. Let the camera and any text read continuous time, not the drawing index. Only the stroke follows the cadence.
  4. Do not change a required delivery rate (24, 25, 30) to imitate a source video. Keep 12 drawings a second inside the file.

This is our proposed implementation. The tutorial does not publish its code; see the source limits in HyperFrames tutorial study.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 08:22.

title: Technique: a camera that is a curve of time
label: Camera curves
summary: Give a 3D camera a few channels, key each one, and join the keys with monotone Hermite curves: smooth, no overshoot, flat on holds, and a pure function of time.

blocks.html:
Technique: a camera that is a curve of time

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Our own Tabletop Miniature style (approved on October 1, 2026) is one small 3D model on a dark table, rendered in real time with Three.js and exported through HyperFrames. There are no cuts: one orbiting camera flies from station to station. The camera is a pure function of time, built from keyframed channels.

blocks.caption: One camera channel, the azimuth, keyed at four stations with two holds. Dashed: linear keys (corners). Orange: a Catmull-Rom spline (dips below the first key, rises above the second). Blue: monotone Hermite. On the right the monotone curve drives the camera around the model.

blocks.html:
How it works

The rig has four numbers: a target point, an azimuth (angle around the model), an elevation and a distance. Every channel is a list of keys joined by curves; the style also keys its post-processing values (blur band, blur radius, depth aperture) in the same table. At time t the renderer reads each channel and places the camera. Nothing else moves it.

The choice of curve matters. A linear join has a corner at every key: the camera starts and stops abruptly. A general spline is smooth but can overshoot: next to a hold it backs up before moving, or swings past the station. A monotone cubic Hermite curve (Fritsch and Carlson) picks its tangents so that the curve never leaves the range of the two keys around it, and has a zero slope on a hold (Wikipedia: monotone cubic interpolation). A hold in the keys is a real hold in the picture.

How to build it

function monotone(xs, ys) {                      // Fritsch-Carlson tangents + cubic Hermite
  const d = xs.slice(1).map((x, i) => (ys[i + 1] - ys[i]) / (x - xs[i]));
  const m = [d[0], ...d.slice(1).map((v, i) => (d[i] * v <= 0 ? 0 : (d[i] + v) / 2)), d.at(-1)];
  d.forEach((di, i) => {
    if (di === 0) { m[i] = m[i + 1] = 0; return; }
    const a = m[i] / di, b = m[i + 1] / di, s = a * a + b * b;
    if (s > 9) { m[i] = (3 / Math.sqrt(s)) * a * di; m[i + 1] = (3 / Math.sqrt(s)) * b * di; }
  });
  return (x) => hermite(xs, ys, m, x);           // standard cubic Hermite basis on the segment
}
const az = monotone(T, AZ), el = monotone(T, EL), dist = monotone(T, DIST);
const camera = (t) => placeOnSphere(target(t), az(t), el(t), dist(t));   // the only place the camera moves

Key the angle as an unwrapped number (350 degrees then 380, not 350 then 20), or the camera spins the long way round. Render camera(frame / fps) for every frame.

Watch for

  • Sight lines at every key. The style page lists it as a trap: a tall prop between the camera path and a station hides it. Check the view at each key, not only the model.
  • Things with a front. Props with a front and a back must face the side the camera passes; check from the camera azimuth.
  • Anchored labels. Tags fixed in 3D can land under the headline at some angles; clamp their screen position.
  • Glare. A bright surface seen top-down can look milky: lower exposure at those keys.
  • One clock. Overlays on the page read the same t, so they stay with the camera; see seekable frame.

Sources: our Tabletop Miniature style page (built with Three.js r181 and HyperFrames, one video made from it); the curve is the standard monotone cubic interpolation. The demo draws all three curves from the same keys. The code above is a sketch we have not run.

title: Technique: closed-form springs
label: Closed-form springs
summary: Move things with the exact step response of a spring, a formula of time, and give the camera a slower spring than the shape.

blocks.html:
Technique: closed-form springs

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The prompts that ask for a premium UI feel agree on how things should move: with springs, and with numbers, not adjectives. One prompt gives them: the shape uses damping 0.72 and settles in 0.35 s, the camera uses damping 1.0 and settles in 0.6 s (flxrnc). It also asks for the inputs "in hex codes, seconds, damping ratios and pixel sizes instead of adjectives". Two other prompts ask for "springs everywhere, a tiny overshoot at most" (AnnaCher, 0xnicc0).

blocks.caption: Both curves are exact formulas, replayed here three times slower than real time. The shape (blue) overshoots by 3.8 % and settles in 0.35 s. The camera (orange) does not overshoot and arrives at 0.6 s.

blocks.html:
How it works

A spring does not need a physics loop. Its response to a step has a closed form, so the value at time t is one expression. That keeps the animation a pure function of time: seeking to any moment needs no simulation of the moments before it.

The two numbers mean what they say. Damping below 1 overshoots a little and returns; at 1 the value arrives without overshoot. Settle time is how long until it stays within 2 % of the target. In the demo, 0.72 gives about 3.8 % overshoot, which reads as life without looking like a cartoon.

Give the camera a slower, non-overshooting spring than the shape. The shape arrives first, then the frame comes to rest around it, and the eye follows the object before the view settles.

How to build it

// step response, 0 to 1. zeta = damping ratio, settle = seconds to stay within 2 %
function spring(t, zeta, settle) {
  if (t <= 0) return 0;
  if (zeta >= 1) { const w = 5.83 / settle; return 1 - (1 + w * t) * Math.exp(-w * t); }
  const w = 4 / (zeta * settle), r = Math.sqrt(1 - zeta * zeta), wd = w * r;
  return 1 - Math.exp(-zeta * w * t) * (Math.cos(wd * t) + (zeta / r) * Math.sin(wd * t));
}

// one spring per change of target, summed, so the value stays a function of t
const value = changes.reduce((v, c) => v + (c.to - c.from) * spring(t - c.at, 0.72, 0.35), start);

Both prompts that animate a main shape ask for this: "when a value changes target several times, add one spring per change" (0xnicc0).

Watch for

  • Bounce. Damping near 0.3 looks like rubber. The prompts keep overshoot small and ban "bouncy cartoon easing".
  • One spring for everything. Give shape, camera and text their own numbers, or the scene moves as one lump.
  • Easing curves for the camera. A cubic ease has no memory of an earlier move; a spring per change blends them.

Sources: flxrnc-251921, annacher-152174, 0xnicc0-516612 in our prompt database. The numbers 0.72, 0.35, 1.0 and 0.6 are the prompt's; the formula and the 3.8 % figure are ours.

title: Technique: construction lines and broken strokes
label: Construction lines
summary: Leave the artist's scaffolding in the picture: faint guides under the contour, and a contour made of short strokes with gaps.

blocks.html:
Technique: construction lines and broken strokes

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A real sketch shows how it was made: a light box, a cross to find the centre, a looser first circle, then a darker contour that does not quite close. ProdAdvice lists "broken strokes" and "light construction lines" among the marks that give the handmade impression (08:05). Studio Igor's whale cartoon draws blue construction strokes before the main action (0:49).

blocks.caption: One circle in three stages: guides (a dashed box, a cross and a looser circle), then a contour of seven short strokes with gaps, then both together with the guides left faint.

blocks.html:
How it works

  • Guides go down first and in a second colour, so they read as scaffolding. A dashed bounding box, a cross through the centre and a slightly larger, looser circle are enough.
  • The contour is split into short strokes. In the demo there are seven, each ending a little before the next begins, with the end points moved by a seeded offset.
  • Together: when the contour lands, the guides drop to about half their strength (opacity 0.9 to 0.45 in the demo) and stay.

The order matters for motion. Guides appear first, which gives the eye something to track; the strokes then arrive over them. A guide that appears after the contour looks like an error.

How to build it

Treat guides as their own layer with their own opacity token. The contour function takes a stroke count and a gap size, and returns a path with several sub-paths:

const strokes = 7, gap = 0.16;   // radians left open at each seam
for (let s = 0; s < strokes; s++) {
  const a0 = (s / strokes) * TAU + gap / 2, a1 = ((s + 1) / strokes) * TAU - gap / 2;
  path.push(arc(cx, cy, r, a0, a1, jitter(seed + s)));
}

Watch for

  • Guides that compete with a label. Keep them out of the area reserved for text, or fade them out before the label arrives.
  • Gaps that look like a rendering bug. If a seam is wider than a few pixels at delivery size, reduce the gap.
  • Everything at once. Use guides on the hero object, not on every element of the frame.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 08:05-09:09, and Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk at 0:49-2:31. Stroke count, gap and opacity figures are from our demo.

title: Technique: an error log that turns into checks
label: Error log
summary: Keep a short list of concrete failures and the rule each one produced, so the next scene starts stronger without a longer prompt.

blocks.html:
Technique: an error log that turns into checks

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The last item on ProdAdvice's checklist is a list of errors (10:14). Studio Igor shows it working: when a character's hand goes behind the body while aiming upward, he adds a corrective rule to the skill (14:14). A mistake is paid for once and then guarded against.

blocks.caption: Three concrete failures and the check each produces: a label collides with the phone crop at 3.2 s (keep labels 90 px inside the safe area), hatching flips direction between frames (one angle per object, fixed seed), text flickers as the contour redraws (labels follow continuous time).

blocks.html:
How it works

Each entry has two halves:

  • What went wrong, specific enough that someone else can find it: the thing, the symptom and the time.
  • The check it becomes, a rule a script or an assistant can apply before it shows you anything.

Good entries name numbers and times. "Label collides with phone crop at 3.2 s" is useful; "text layout issues" is not. A vague entry cannot become a check.

Keep it short

Do not paste an ever-growing transcript into every prompt. Cap the log at the failures that still matter, merge entries that say the same thing, and move a rule that is always true into the style contract. Version the file with the project, so a revert brings back the matching rules.

Make it run

The best rules are tested, not just read:

if (label.box.right > frame.width - 90) fail("label inside safe area", label.id, time);

A rule that can fail loudly in the render step needs no one to remember it.

Watch for

  • Rules that fight each other. When two checks disagree, decide which wins and delete the other.
  • A log nobody feeds. Add the entry in the same sitting as the fix, while the frame number is still in front of you.
  • Rules from a different format. A check made for a map fact may not fit a character scene. Note the scope in the entry.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 10:14-11:41; Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk at 14:14-17:33. The three example entries are from our HyperFrames tutorial study and are illustrations.

title: Technique: feedback in passes
label: Feedback passes
summary: Improve a coded video in short passes, one concern at a time: pace, then sound, then music fitted to the beat.

blocks.html:
Technique: feedback in passes

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The tutorial's promo was not one prompt but a process: install HyperFrames, ask for key frames, tell it to keep to the brand and give your references, then refine step by step. First feedback on which scenes are too fast, then sound and music (a few options to choose from), after which the model fitted the animation to the music so it hooks harder (ИИ МАСТОДОНТ, 08:13). Other demos in the same video: the vertical Short took feedback such as "redraw the logo, fast in places, slow in others", and the talking-head edit began dull and improved when he asked it to be creative and not follow a template (09:15, 11:07). A prompt in our database reports the same shape: "1 prompt and 2 rounds of feedback" (daniel_haida).

blocks.caption: Three versions. v1 has only picture, with the note that scenes are too fast. v2 adds sound to every movement. v3 adds a track cut to its beat. Each pass adds one layer.

blocks.html:
How it works

A model that is asked for everything at once spreads its effort thin. One concern per pass keeps each change small enough to judge. The order matters: pace first (picture), then sound that matches visible movement, then music, which depends on pace being settled. Each pass starts from the last approved version and is checked with render and inspect.

How to build it

  • Pass 1: "scenes 2 and 4 are too fast; hold each for at least 1.5 s". Re-check the timing plan.
  • Pass 2: "add a sound for every visible movement" (the prompt database has one: "make every sound match a movement you can see", adrianduta96).
  • Pass 3: bring your own track or generate one without words, and ask to fit the video to the song and pick the best moments (13:37). Put the cuts on the beat grid.
  • When it feels flat: ask it to be creative and not follow a template.

Watch for

  • Mixed notes. "Faster, add music and change the colour" is three passes; the model will do one well.
  • Music first. Changing pace afterwards breaks the fit.
  • Music made in code. The author says he does not know how the model makes it and prefers his own track; one prompt in our database makes the soundtrack from sine waves and noise (daniel_haida). Treat either as a draft to listen to.

Sources: ИИ МАСТОДОНТ, yEpN_s9UkAE at 08:13, 09:15, 11:07 and 13:37; daniel-haida-636937 and adrianduta96-992248 in our prompt database.

title: Technique: shapes as harmonics, and morphing between them
label: Harmonic morph
summary: Store a closed outline as a few complex harmonics, then morph between two outlines by mixing coefficients. The same list is also a smoothness dial.

blocks.html:
Technique: shapes as harmonics, and morphing between them

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

This technique comes from the owner's own project, a set of small browser games where every creature, asteroid and letter is a closed outline stored as Fourier coefficients (the project is private; the maths is standard). The idea fits video as well: an outline is a list of complex numbers, and a list of numbers can be mixed.

blocks.caption: Left, a star becomes a house: the 12 largest harmonics of each outline are mixed from alpha 0 to 1, drawn as 14 in-between frames (dashed: the two full outlines). Right, the same star rebuilt from 2, 6 and 24 harmonics.

blocks.html:
How it works

Walk once around a closed outline at constant speed and write each point as a complex number x + iy. A discrete Fourier transform turns the points into coefficients c_k, one per signed frequency k. The outline comes back as point(t) = sum of c_k * exp(i * 2 * pi * k * t) for t from 0 to 1. The k = 0 term is the centre; k = 1 alone is a circle; each further pair adds finer detail.

Two things follow:

  • Smoothness is a budget. Keep the centre and the few terms with the largest magnitude, and the outline loses its fine corners but keeps its character. This is a low-pass filter on a shape. It is also a size limit: 12 numbers instead of 96 points.
  • A morph is a mix. If two shapes use the same frequencies, mix(a, b, alpha) is a + (b - a) * alpha on the real and imaginary part of each coefficient. A frequency missing on one side counts as zero. Every in-between frame is a valid, smooth outline, and alpha can be eased, sprung or keyed like any other number.

How to build it

Do the DFT once, at authoring time, and keep the coefficients:

const N = 96;                                   // same sample count for every shape
const ca = selectLargest(dft(resample(star,  N)), 12);
const cb = selectLargest(dft(resample(house, N)), 12);

const pose = (t) => contour(mix(ca, cb, easeInOut(t)), 120);   // a pure function of t
ctx.fill(new Path2D(toPath(pose(t))));

resample walks the polygon and returns N points spaced evenly by arc length. selectLargest keeps the centre plus the budget terms of largest magnitude. contour evaluates the sum at m values of t.

Watch for

  • Same start, same direction. Both outlines must run the same way round and start at the corresponding point. The project's own notes warn that automatic alignment by closest point does not guarantee the intended match: look at the middle frames.
  • One fixed set per clip. Pick the harmonics once for the clip. Reselecting the largest terms on every in-between frame makes terms switch on and off and the outline twitch.
  • One normalisation for the whole family. Scale and centre all shapes of a clip the same way, or the morph also resizes.
  • Mid-way self-crossing. Two valid outlines can mix into one that crosses itself. Check frames at alpha 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75.
  • Cost. The plain DFT is quadratic. Fine at authoring time for up to a few hundred samples; do not run it per frame.
  • Corners. A low budget rounds them. That is a look, not a bug, but say so in the style contract.

Sources: the owner's project and its package notes (private repository); the maths is the standard Fourier description of a closed curve. The demo above runs a real DFT on two polygons. We built the demo and did not run a video through this pipeline.

title: Technique: letters as compound harmonic contours
label: Harmonic type
summary: A glyph is a few closed contours. Fill them as one compound path with the even-odd rule so holes stay open, and draw text from the same primitives as the art.

blocks.html:
Technique: letters as compound harmonic contours

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

In the owner's game project the letters are not a font file. Each glyph is a short list of closed contours, stored as harmonics like every other shape (harmonic morph), plus an advance width and an entry and exit point. Text is laid out from those glyphs. The picture and the type then come from one source, with one look.

blocks.caption: The letters O and A, each with an outer and an inner contour rebuilt from 16 harmonics. Non-zero fill (left) fills the holes in; even-odd fill of one compound path (right) keeps them open.

blocks.html:
How it works

An "O" is two contours: the outside and the hole. Draw them as two separate shapes and the hole is covered. Draw them as one path with several sub-paths and the fill rule decides. With the non-zero rule, two contours that run the same way both count as "inside", so the hole fills. With the even-odd rule, a point is inside when a ray from it crosses an odd number of edges, so the hole stays open whichever way the contours run (MDN: fill-rule).

The project draws a glyph as one compound path with even-odd fill, and sizes text through the font's units per em. Spaces use a stored space advance. A missing character is an error, not a silent gap.

How to build it

function glyphPath(glyph, scale, x, y) {
  let d = "";
  for (const c of glyph.contours) d += pathOf(contour(c.harmonics, 96), x, y, scale); // M..L..Z each
  return d;                                    // one string, several sub-paths
}
ctx.fill(new Path2D(glyphPath(g, size, penX, baseline)), "evenodd");
penX += g.advance * size;

A letter animates like any other harmonic shape: its contours can be mixed with another letter's, as long as both have the same number of contours in the same order. Each contour can also go through the kinetic type timing.

Watch for

  • Hole contours too. Every hole is its own contour in the glyph. Forget it and the "A" is a solid triangle.
  • Missing characters. Decide the character set before the first draw; fall back loudly.
  • Baseline and Y direction. The caller owns the baseline and the axis direction. Pick one and test a letter with a descender.
  • Legibility is a visual check. A low harmonic budget rounds the corners and can make "A" and "R" look alike. The project says recognisable silhouettes are acceptance checks for the consuming game, not something numbers can prove.
  • Licensing. Letter shapes you draw yourself are yours; do not trace a font you are not allowed to copy.

Sources: the owner's project (private repository) and its package notes. Our demo builds two letters from polygons through a real DFT. We have not set a full alphabet.

title: Technique: hatching instead of a flat fill
label: Hatching
summary: Shade with strokes, not with a solid colour. A circle-and-chord recipe, a second crossing pass and the reasons it keeps a drawing from looking digital.

blocks.html:
Technique: hatching instead of a flat fill

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A flat fill is the clearest sign of a computer-made drawing. A pencil shades by laying down many short parallel strokes, and the viewer reads their spacing as light and dark. ProdAdvice shows this as a diagram that contrasts a flat fill with hatched shading (09:00).

blocks.caption: The same ball twice. Left, a flat fill. Right, diagonal strokes only on the side away from the light, then a second pass crossing the darkest part.

blocks.html:
How it works

  1. Decide where the light comes from. In the demo it is the upper left, so the shadow is on the lower right.
  2. Lay parallel strokes at one angle (45 degrees here), spaced 6 px apart, only where the surface is in shadow. Each stroke runs from one edge of the shape to the other.
  3. Add a second pass at the crossing angle over the deepest part only. Two directions read as a darker tone than one.
  4. Wobble each stroke slightly with a seeded offset (1.6 px in the demo), so the lines are not machine-straight. Draw the strokes on in order, not all at once, if the shape appears by being drawn.

How to build it

For a circle the strokes are chords. Lines x + y = k cut a circle of radius r at distance d = |cx + cy - k| / sqrt(2) from its centre, with half-length sqrt(r * r - d * d), so no clipping mask is needed. For other shapes, clip a set of long diagonal lines to the shape and keep those on the shadow side.

Spacing is the tone control. Closer strokes are darker, so a gradient of shade is a gradient of spacing, not of opacity.

Watch for

  • Hatching that changes direction between frames. Fix the angle per object and seed the offsets; see Drawing cadence and a stable seed. Put this failure in your error log.
  • Shading under text. Keep the area behind a label free of strokes, or the label loses contrast.
  • Too many strokes. A busy shape competes with the message. Reserve the dense hatch for one object.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 08:05-09:09. The chord arithmetic and the spacing values are from our demo.

title: Technique: a clock per motion, accumulated
label: Independent clocks
summary: Change a speed without moving the past: advance each motion's own phase by speed times dt, and give every motion its own clock.

blocks.html:
Technique: a clock per motion, accumulated

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The owner's game project moves planets around stars and spins them. Its notes state the rule: orbit and spin speeds advance independent accumulated clocks, so changing a slider changes only future motion and never recalculates the past at the new speed. The ocean waves keep a third, real-time clock, so stopping a planet's rotation does not freeze the sea. It is a game rule, and it solves a real problem in speed ramps and slow motion.

blocks.caption: Speed goes from 1x to 3x at 2 s. Left: phase = speed(t) * t, so the phase jumps from 2 to 6 at the change. Right: phase += speed * dt, so the phase only changes slope.

blocks.html:
How it works

If a motion is written as angle = speed * t, changing speed at 2 s re-scales everything before it: at the moment of the change the angle jumps from 1 * 2 to 3 * 2. The picture pops. The fix is to store the phase itself and advance it: phase += speed * dt. A change of speed now bends the curve and leaves its past alone. Each motion has its own phase (orbit, spin, waves, a camera drift), so you can slow one without touching the others.

For video the phase must still be a function of time, or seeking breaks. Phase is the integral of speed, so build a table once and read it:

const fps = 30, phase = new Float64Array(frames + 1);
for (let f = 1; f <= frames; f++) phase[f] = phase[f - 1] + speed((f - 0.5) / fps) / fps;
// renderAt(t) reads phase[Math.floor(t * fps)], or interpolates between two entries

Keep one table per motion. A speed ramp is then a few keys in speed(t) (eased with springs or a Hermite curve), never a step.

Watch for

  • Step changes of speed. A step in speed is a step in velocity: a visible kick. Ramp it over a few frames.
  • Loops. A seamless loop needs the phase to come back to a multiple of one turn at the end; check the table's last entry.
  • Sound. If the sound follows the motion, drive it from the same phase table.
  • Slow motion. A slow-down is a lower speed for a while. Do not render at a lower frame rate and stretch it; use subframe blur if the motion needs it.

Sources: the owner's project notes on celestial motion (private repository). The table code is our proposal; we have not rendered a clip with it.

title: Technique: kinetic type per glyph
label: Kinetic type per glyph
summary: Treat every letter as its own element with its own spring and a fixed stagger, so words arrive as a rhythm and not as a block.

blocks.html:
Technique: kinetic type per glyph

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

One prompt in our database spells out how a poster-style word should arrive: "per-glyph spring (y, opacity, blur). Stagger = 1/16 note at 120 BPM (125 ms)" (techhalla). The same prompt asks for a slam from below with spring overshoot for the opening line, and for letters that scramble (a seeded shuffle per glyph) and then snap into place on the beat. Another asks for the wordmark to rise letter by letter from a mask line (0xnicc0).

blocks.caption: Each letter of STEAL is its own element and rises 125 ms after the one before. The ticks under the word are the start offsets: 0, 125, 250, 375 and 500 ms.

blocks.html:
How it works

A word that fades in as one block has one motion. A word whose letters start 125 ms apart has a rhythm, and the rhythm locks to the beat grid: at 120 BPM, 125 ms is a sixteenth note, so the last letter still lands within the beat. Each glyph carries three animated values (vertical offset, opacity, blur), each from its own spring started at start + index * 0.125.

How to build it

const STAGGER = 0.125;                              // 1/16 note at 120 BPM
for (const [i, g] of glyphs.entries()) {
  const k = spring(t - (start + i * STAGGER), 0.72, 0.35);
  drawGlyph(g, { y: (1 - k) * 40, alpha: k, blur: (1 - k) * 12 });
}

For the scramble variant, shuffle with a seeded shuffle per glyph, never Math.random.

Watch for

  • Too many words. The same prompt limits the display type to one to four words.
  • Stagger longer than the beat. Forty letters at 125 ms take five seconds; stagger by word, not by letter, for long lines.
  • Blur you cannot read. Keep the final frame crisp; blur is for the first 150 ms.

Sources: techhalla-498547, 0xnicc0-516612 in our prompt database; the snippet is ours.

title: Technique: painted layers, with light and text in code
label: Layered assets
summary: Generate the detailed pictures as separate transparent layers, then let code do depth, light, particles and text. Parallax is the proof it works.

blocks.html:
Technique: painted layers, with light and text in code

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Studio Igor's first platformer, drawn entirely in code, scored 2/10; he stopped after 37 minutes and 12 % of a weekly model allowance. His second attempt generated the pictures as images and let code move them (6:09). The split is the technique: images carry painted forms and texture, code carries scale, position, light, motion and interaction (7:48).

blocks.caption: Background, subject and foreground are images; light and text are code. Composed, a slow sideways camera moves the foreground by 18 px, the subject by 9 px and the background by 4 px (demo values) while the code layer stays still.

blocks.html:
How it works

  • Separate by depth. Generate the background, the subject and the foreground as their own layers, each on a transparent ground with room around the subject.
  • Keep mutable effects out of the pictures. Glow, shadow, particles, text and water are deliberately excluded from generated images (19:12). Draw them in code, where one number changes them.
  • Move layers by depth. When the camera shifts sideways, near layers shift more than far ones. That is parallax, and it is what makes flat pictures read as a space.
  • Hold text still. Text belongs to the code layer, so it never slides with the picture.

Check before you animate

  • Holes. When a layer moves, look for gaps at its edges. Draw layers wider than the frame, as the demo does.
  • A clean subject. Neutral light and no baked shadow, so the lighting you add does not fight the lighting in the picture.
  • A recorded source. Save each asset with its prompt, model and source reference, so a bad layer can be regenerated.

Limits

The method suits scenes and cutout characters. Studio Igor rejected AI sprite sheets and cutting one generated character into pieces; he generates separate body parts in an agreed pose and assembles them (19:12). It is not a replacement for frame animation, and the allowance percentages are one creator's account, not a transferable cost.

Details and a proposed experiment for a 5 to 10 s shot are in Layered art tutorial study. The author's open ref2game skill describes the workflow.

Source: Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk at 6:09-8:59 and 19:12-20:55. The pixel shifts in the demo are illustrative.

title: Technique: line boil, a contour that is redrawn while the shape stays still
label: Line boil
summary: Redraw each outline a dozen times a second with a little wobble, so a still pose looks hand-drawn. How it works, a small code recipe and where it goes wrong.

blocks.html:
Technique: line boil

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Hand-drawn animation never repeats a line exactly. Even a character holding still has an outline that trembles, because the artist redraws it for every drawing. Line boil copies that on purpose: the silhouette stays where it is, and only the stroke is redrawn, about 12 times a second.

blocks.caption: One circle, six drawings. On the left they play in turn, one every 83 ms, which is 12 drawings a second; on the right the same six are laid over each other. The shape does not move, only its edge does.

blocks.html:
How it works

Two things move on different clocks. The object (its position, size, rotation) follows the scene timeline smoothly. The outline of that object is a separate set of points, and those points are displaced by a small random amount, a new amount for each drawing. ProdAdvice describes exactly this for "otherwise still contours" at 12 fps (08:05), and Studio Igor's whale cartoon uses the same effect with "vibrating contours" at about 12 drawings a second (0:49).

The displacement is small. In the demo above it is 2.6 px on a circle of 62 px radius, which is about 4 % of the radius. A larger amount reads as shaking, not as pencil.

How to build it

Our own recipe, not recovered source code:

// one drawing = the same points, each moved by a seeded random offset
function boil(points, drawing, amp, sceneSeed) {
  const rand = mulberry32(sceneSeed + drawing);
  return points.map(([x, y]) => [x + (rand() - 0.5) * 2 * amp, y + (rand() - 0.5) * 2 * amp]);
}
const drawing = Math.floor(time * 12);   // the drawing cadence
draw(boil(outline, drawing, 2.6, 7));

Keep the position of the object outside this function. Pass the amplitude as one token of the style (see Style contract), so one number changes the whole film.

Watch for

  • Noise everywhere. Move only the strokes, never the labels or numbers. A label that wobbles is hard to read.
  • Too large an amplitude. If the shape seems to swim, halve the amount.
  • A drawing rhythm tied to the file. The drawing index must come from time, not from the frame number. See Drawing cadence and a stable seed.
  • Sparkle. Judge it at normal playback speed, not frame by frame. A single frame always looks fine.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g, and Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk; both are analysed in HyperFrames tutorial study and Layered art tutorial study. The amplitude figure is from our demo, not from either video.

title: Technique: a locked message and a ban list
label: Locked message and bans
summary: Fix the exact words and their order, and list what must not appear, so the model spends its effort on motion and not on inventing copy.

blocks.html:
Technique: a locked message and a ban list

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The most precise prompt in our database does two things that cost nothing and remove most of the risk. It locks the message: six lines "in this exact order", with the instruction "do not soften, do not add filler slogans", and small supporting words (at most 18 characters, never full sentences). And it bans a list: "generic AI clichés (brains, robots, neural nets, sparkles), soft gradients, bouncy cartoon easing, particle explosions, stock futuristic HUD, long paragraphs, narrator essay energy, Canva-deck energy, extra slogans, purple/blue neon, glassmorphism" (techhalla). Other prompts ban the same family: "crossfades, gradients on UI, particles, glows, bouncy easing, dead beats, anything that feels like a template" (0xnicc0).

blocks.caption: Left: six lines of text in a fixed order, the only words allowed on screen. Right: a ban list, each item struck through.

blocks.html:
How it works

A model left alone adds slogans and decoration. A locked message takes the writing away from it, so all its effort goes into timing, type and camera. A ban list does the opposite job: it removes the generic defaults that make a piece look made by a template. Together with strict numbers (a palette of three hex values, three named fonts, tracking values) they leave little room for a generic result.

How to build it

  • Write the lines first and number them; each line gets one beat on the beat grid.
  • Put them in the style contract with palette and fonts as values.
  • Add the ban list as a check in the error log: after each render, look for anything on the list.
  • Keep it short; the prompt's list has about a dozen items, not fifty.

Watch for

  • A message locked too early. Lock it after you are sure of the story; changing it later is a rewrite.
  • Bans without a reason. A list the model does not understand gets worked around. Say what to do instead (for example, "springs, tiny overshoot at most").
  • Copy you did not write. A locked line you did not write still needs a source and a check; see auditing a video.

Sources: techhalla-498547, 0xnicc0-516612 in our prompt database. We have read the prompts, not run them.

title: Technique: a reveal through the letters
label: Mask reveal
summary: Replace one line of text with the next by turning the outgoing word into a window, so the cut is made by the type itself.

blocks.html:
Technique: a reveal through the letters

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

One prompt describes a transition that needs no cross-fade: "BAD PROMPTING IS" replaces the previous line "via mask wipe through the letterforms (the outgoing line is the mask)", with a magenta and green channel split on the cut. The required technique is stated plainly: "destination text revealed by animating a path mask derived from the outgoing word's outlines" (techhalla).

blocks.caption: Left: the outgoing plate with the word BAD. Middle: the word becomes a window and the next scene shows through the letterforms. Right: the window grows until the next scene fills the frame.

blocks.html:
How it works

The old word is on a plate. To leave, the plate gets a hole in the shape of the word. Through the hole you see the next scene. Then the hole grows (the letters scale up) until the plate is gone. The viewer sees one object, the word, doing the cutting, so the change reads as designed, not as a fade. The mask path is derived from the same outlines that drew the word, so the two cannot drift apart.

How to build it

In SVG or Canvas, draw the destination, then the plate with the outgoing text as a cut-out:

<mask id="m"><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#fff"/>
  <text id="word" fill="#000" font-size="54">BAD</text></mask>
<rect class="destination"/>                     <!-- next scene -->
<rect class="plate" mask="url(#m)"/>            <!-- outgoing scene, with the word cut out -->

Drive font-size (or a scale on the text in the mask) from a spring of time, so the reveal stays seekable. Add the misregistration on the cut frame.

Watch for

  • A thin face. A light font makes a window too small to see through; use a heavy display font, as the prompt does (Archivo Black).
  • Mask and word out of step. Use the same size, tracking and position for both.
  • A fade as a fallback. If the mask is not ready, cut instead; do not fade.

Source: techhalla-498547 in our prompt database. We have read the prompt, not run it; the demo is our drawing.

title: Technique: print misregistration
label: Print misregistration
summary: Show two offset colour copies of text for a moment on impact frames only, like a badly aligned print.

blocks.html:
Technique: print misregistration

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A street-poster look can be made with a cheap trick from print: two ink colours that do not line up. The prompt says when and how much: "on accent frames only, duplicate the text layer offset (±2–4 px) in magenta and acid green at 40% opacity", and "magenta and green may misregister (print offset) by 2 to 4 px on impact frames only" (techhalla).

blocks.caption: At the two impact marks a blue and an orange copy of IMPACT appear behind the word, offset 4 px at 45 % opacity, then vanish. Between impacts the text is clean.

blocks.html:
How it works

The offset copies add a hit to a beat: they make an impact look physical. The rule "impact frames only" matters as much as the effect. If the colour split is always on, it is a style filter; if it appears on the beat and disappears, it is an accent. The values are small on purpose: 2 to 4 px at 40 %.

How to build it

function drawTitle(t) {
  drawText(ink, 0, 0);                        // the clean text
  const hit = impact(t);                      // 1 on an impact frame, 0 otherwise (from the beat grid)
  if (hit) {
    drawText(accentA, -3, 0, 0.4);            // behind, offset left
    drawText(accentB, +3, +2, 0.4);           // behind, offset right
  }
}

Take impact(t) from the beat grid and keep it to a few frames.

Watch for

  • Always on. It stops reading as an impact.
  • Large offsets. Past about 4 px the text becomes hard to read at phone size.
  • Wrong palette. The prompt pairs two accent colours with one dark background and one white; other hues are banned.

Source: techhalla-498547 in our prompt database; the snippet is ours.

title: Technique: a number as a readout, not a slam
label: Number readout
summary: Show a figure small, beside the thing it measures, on the spoken word, with a thin measuring line. It reads as evidence, not as decoration.

blocks.html:
Technique: a number as a readout, not a slam

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

In the demo from Andrey Zenin's tutorial, every number is an instrument readout (2:26). A thin measuring line and "50 M" stand beside a drop tower. The text is about 3 % of the frame height, not a headline.

blocks.caption: The same drop tower in two portrait frames. Left, a slam: a large "50 M" over the picture, 8 % of the frame height. Right, a readout: a thin measuring line and a small "50 M" beside the tower, 3.5 % of the frame height.

blocks.html:
How it works

  • Attach it to the thing measured. Put the label beside the object and draw the measuring line along it. The number then says what it is without a caption.
  • Make it small. In our rebuild a readout is 60 to 80 px on a 1920 px frame, which is 3.1 to 4.2 %; the drawing uses 3.5 %. The v3 bond Short set "US$8.8" as a slam of 156 px, which is 8.1 %.
  • Land it on the word. The readout arrives when the number is spoken, without a slam or a bounce.
  • One per shot, at most. The demo's other readouts are "TREMOR 0.0", "VOICE" with an even level meter and "100 %" on a popcorn bucket. Each confirms or contradicts the voice.
  • No captions and no headline type in the excerpt.

How to build it

const readout = { label: "50 M", size: 0.035 * frameHeight, at: wordStart("fifty") };

Make the label and the measuring line one component, so the line and the text always move and fade together.

Watch for

  • Unreadable on a phone. Test at arm's length. If it fails, make it slightly larger, not a slam.
  • A count-up on a ratio. Mid-count it shows a wrong ratio on screen (the bond Short builder saw "1 : 8" on the way to a different value). Show finished ratios.
  • A number the voice already says, with a label that repeats the voice. Keep a label only where the voice cannot carry the meaning.

This is a proposed change for our shorts, not an approved style rule; it was suggested in Reference: 2D video plugin and has not been audited.

Source: Andrey Zenin, YyUP_hSovOg at 2:26-2:47; Skill trial: bond Short for the count-up finding.

title: Technique: one shape, never cut
label: One shape, never cut
summary: Tell a product story with one element that morphs from state to state, driven by a cursor, with no cuts and no cross-fades.

blocks.html:
Technique: one shape, never cut

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A group of prompts for product UI motion share a rule: one shape tells the whole story. "Every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a short blur" (AnnaCher). "A prompt bar becomes a button, the button becomes a progress ring, the ring becomes a preview window... No cuts, no fades between scenes: objects transform" (0xnicc0). "One shape, zero cuts. The shape morphs from state to state and is never replaced" (flxrnc).

blocks.caption: One element in four states, from a mascot to a play button, a loader and a timeline. The dashed ring travels between the cards to show the element is the same one: it morphs and is never replaced.

blocks.html:
How it works

Because the element persists, the eye follows it across states and the story needs no cut. Size, radius and colour are each a chain of springs, so a change in one state starts from wherever the last one ended. Content inside the shape is separate: it swaps with a 12 px blur and a fade over 0.15 s (flxrnc), and needs its own clip and its own enter and exit timing so text never overlaps (0xnicc0). A cursor causes every change with a real click or drag, and its tip stays locked to whatever it drags. The camera zooms so each state fills about half the frame.

How to build it

const shape = {
  w: chain(springs, "w"), h: chain(springs, "h"),
  r: chain(springs, "r"), color: chain(springs, "color"),
};
// at time t, read each property; draw one rounded rect; then draw the current content inside its clip

List the states and their beats first, as in the storyboard.

Watch for

  • Cross-fading one colour into another. The prompt says: do not cross-fade orange into ink. Animate the colour value.
  • Content popping while the shape moves. Give text its own timing, after the morph has started.
  • A cursor that arrives late. Aim it at where the target will be when it lands, and keep its speed under 65 px per frame.

Sources: annacher-152174, 0xnicc0-516612, flxrnc-251921 in our prompt database. We have not run these prompts; the demo is a stand-in drawing, not their output.

title: Technique: reference by link
label: Reference by link
summary: Give the assistant a link to a clip you like and ask for your own story in that style, instead of describing the style in words.

blocks.html:
Technique: reference by link

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The ИИ МАСТОДОНТ tutorial lists this as the first of its four tips: when you see a strong clip, give the link to the post to the model and say "do it in this style, but with my story or prompt"; the author calls it the simplest way to copy any style, and says it used to be almost impossible (13:10). He shows it in the cartoon demo, where he pasted a prompt and a link to an X post, and the model went and found the media itself, which older models needed a file path for (03:45). For the promo he gave references, then sent the model to look for the best videos made with the same model, "for inspiration", and it came back with a better result (07:23). Several prompts in our database do the same: "Analyze [a link] and build a product promo from our own UI" (AnnaCher).

blocks.caption: A link goes in; a short read-out of the style comes out (palette, type, camera, beat grid, cursor, springs); then it is applied to a new story.

blocks.html:
How it works

Style is hard to put in words and easy to point at. The model reads the clip or its post and extracts a specification: colours, fonts, camera behaviour, timing grid, how the cursor moves. Your content (words, facts, product) is separate. That is the whole contract: their grammar of motion, your story.

How to build it

Ask in two steps so you can check the read-out:

  1. "Read this post and write the style as a spec: palette in hex, fonts, camera moves, tempo, cursor rules, what is banned."
  2. "Now make my 12 s piece about X with that spec." Keep the spec in the style contract so every scene uses it.

Watch for

  • Copying the content. The link supplies style only. Check that no copyrighted frames, words or music came along; see the style gate.
  • A read-out you did not see. Without step 1 you cannot tell whether the model understood the reference.
  • Taking a demo for a guarantee. The author says a good monteur still does better; treat the result as a draft (11:14).

Sources: ИИ МАСТОДОНТ, yEpN_s9UkAE at 03:45, 07:23 and 13:10 (transcript read by us; we have not run the prompts), and annacher-152174 in our prompt database.

title: Technique: render, then inspect real frames
label: Render and inspect
summary: A quality gate that cannot be argued with: pull frames at fixed times from an actual render, write down what is wrong with each, fix the source.

blocks.html:
Technique: render, then inspect real frames

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The creator credits his model with analysing reference clips and checking its own work (05:00), and his checklist includes an agent review of frames (10:14). Studio Igor adds numbers: scripts measure foot slide, asymmetry, bone stretch and transition jolts, and image critics look at rendered frames (20:55). The shared idea is that an assistant's statement that "it looks right" is not evidence; a frame is.

blocks.caption: Frames at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 4.5 s are checked in turn. The 2.0 s frame has its label at the edge; the defect is logged with its time, the source is fixed and the clip is rendered again.

blocks.html:
How it works

  1. Render a preview of the scene, not a mock-up. A saved file is the proof that the check ran.
  2. Pull frames at fixed times: the opening, a midpoint, a transition and the last frame. For a 5 s clip that is 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 4.5 s.
  3. Write one observation per frame, with the time. "Label touches the right edge at 2.0 s" is a finding. "Looks fine" is not.
  4. Fix the source, not the frame, then render again and compare.
  5. Watch the clip once at normal speed. Frames cannot show sparkle, flicker, a missed beat or a bad hold.

A person still decides about meaning, facts and style fit. The loop removes the defects an assistant can see and hands over a short list of what remains.

Add numbers where you can

Measure what is measurable: contour displacement per frame, text bounding boxes against the safe area, the share of near-black frames. Our skill trial turned scans like these into gates, and every build failed at least one gate in a draft and was fixed before the render.

Watch for

  • A claim without a file. Require the preview path and the frame times in the report.
  • Checking only the start. Defects cluster at transitions and at the end.
  • Fixing in post. A patched frame hides a source that will break again; correct the scene.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 05:00-06:16 and 10:14-11:41; Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk at 20:55-22:50. Both describe the checks; neither publishes pass rates.

title: Technique: a seamless loop
label: Seamless loop
summary: Make the last frame equal the first, including the cursor, so a piece can repeat with no visible seam.

blocks.html:
Technique: a seamless loop

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Looping pieces need more than a long fade at the end. Three prompts in our database require "the last frame must be the first frame" (flxrnc, AnnaCher, 0xnicc0), and one adds that position, opacity and cursor must match too (techhalla). The same prompt that asks for a 14 s loop lists the usual failure as a fix: "the cursor jump at the loop wrap" is removed with t - 14*floor(t/14).

blocks.caption: Two 14 s loops drawn as rings. Left: the last frame is not the first, and the dot jumps at the seam. Right: time is wrapped and the last frame equals the first, so the dot closes the ring.

blocks.html:
How it works

A loop has a seam where the end meets the start. Anything that is not identical at the two ends shows as a jump: a cursor that ends mid-screen, an opacity that has not returned to its starting value, a spring that has not settled. The fix has two halves. Design the story so it returns to its first state (in the prompts, "the toast turns back into an empty prompt bar", "the toast shrinks back into the mascot"). And make every time-dependent value read the wrapped time, so a frame at t = 14 is the frame at t = 0.

How to build it

const LOOP = 14;
const wrap = (t) => t - LOOP * Math.floor(t / LOOP);   // 0 <= wrap(t) < 14
window.renderAt = (t) => draw(ctx, layout(plan, wrap(t)));

Then compare frame 0 with the last frame, pixel by pixel, as one of the render-and-inspect checks. Let all springs finish before the end so the last frame is at rest.

Watch for

  • A cursor that ends elsewhere. Park it where it starts, as part of the last beat.
  • A long cross-fade. It hides the jump but also the story; one prompt bans "crossfades" outright (0xnicc0).
  • Springs still moving. A spring that settles at 0.35 s needs 0.35 s of quiet before the wrap.

Sources: flxrnc-251921, annacher-152174, 0xnicc0-516612, techhalla-498547 in our prompt database. The wrap expression is the prompt's; the pixel comparison is our proposal.

title: Technique: a seekable frame function
label: Seekable frame
summary: Write the whole picture as renderAt(t), a pure function of time, so any moment can be frozen, checked and re-rendered exactly.

blocks.html:
Technique: a seekable frame function

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Several of the strongest prompts in our prompt database make the same demand first: the picture at time t may depend on t and nothing else. One prompt states it as a build rule: window.renderAt(t) must be a pure function of time, with no Math.random, no clock and no carried state, and ?t= in the address must freeze the exact moment (flxrnc). Another asks for seek(t) with no CSS transitions, no setInterval and no React state across frames (techhalla). A third says the same in one line: every frame is a function (BuildFastWithAI).

blocks.caption: Top row: five frames computed from time alone, so a jump to 3.6 s gives the right picture. Bottom row: each frame is built from the last one, so after the same jump the ball is still where it was at 2.4 s.

blocks.html:
How it works

If a frame depends only on t, three things become cheap. You can seek: open ?t=3.6 and see exactly that moment. You can check: render five stills around a beat without playing the clip (storyboard and pre-pass). You can re-render a single scene and get the same pixels. A stateful animation, where each frame nudges the previous one, gives none of these: a jump lands in a state nobody has computed.

How to build it

Keep every number that changes in a function of t, and draw from it:

window.renderAt = (t) => {
  const p = layout(plan, t);   // positions, opacities, text: from t and the plan only
  draw(ctx, p);                // paint; never read what was painted before
};
const t = Number(new URLSearchParams(location.search).get("t"));
if (!Number.isNaN(t)) renderAt(t);   // ?t=3.6 freezes that moment

The export loop then calls renderAt(frame / fps) for every frame. Randomness comes from a stable seed, never from Math.random.

Watch for

  • Hidden state. A counter, an array that grows, a timer or a transition that keeps running is state. Derive it from t instead (a typed text shows floor(progress * length) characters).
  • CSS transitions and timers. They run on the page clock, not on t. Do not use them.
  • Changing a target several times. Do not mutate a value. Add one spring per change.

Sources: the prompts flxrnc-251921, techhalla-498547 and BuildFastWithAI in our prompt database. We have read the prompts, not run them; the code is our proposal.

title: Technique: one sentence, one shot, cut just before the word
label: Sentence and shot
summary: Cut to a new picture a fraction of a second before its sentence begins, and put the longest pause before the punch line. Measured from a 30 s demo.

blocks.html:
Technique: one sentence, one shot, cut just before the word

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

A code-drawn demo in Andrey Zenin's tutorial shows an editing grammar that carries over to any narrated video (2:02). We measured its 28.6 s excerpt with scene detection and word timestamps; the full table is in Reference: 2D video plugin.

blocks.caption: Four sentences and their four shots on a 10 s axis (illustrative times). Each cut lands 0.14 s before its sentence's first word, and the longest pause (0.8 s) comes before the punch line.

blocks.html:
What the measurement shows

  • After the first, 11 of 13 sentences get a new shot. Ten cut at the sentence start and one on the noun the shot shows. The two without a cut play out inside one held shot where the action itself changes the picture.
  • The cut comes 0.01 to 0.29 s before the first word, with a median of 0.14 s. The eye sees the new picture a few frames before the ear hears the sentence.
  • The pattern is a wide shot, then a close insert of the one detail that carries the sentence. The inserts are short (1.0 to 2.1 s); the wides carry the time (1.6 to 6.0 s).
  • Gaps between sentences run from 0.38 to 0.80 s, with a median near 0.48 s. The 0.80 s gap sits right before the punch line.
  • The camera does not travel. A closer view is a cut to a new framing, not a push.

How to build it

Mark sentence starts separately from word times in your cue file. Put shot boundaries on the sentence starts, 0.1 to 0.3 s early. Word cues inside a sentence drive reveals, not cuts.

shots = sentences.map(s => ({ cutAt: s.start - 0.14, hold: s.end }));

Give the punch line the largest gap_before value. A setup shot shows what everyone expects, a short insert shows what actually happened.

Watch for

  • Cuts inside a sentence, unless the sentence is a list.
  • A locked frame with nothing changing. A static frame is alive only if something inside it changes; our skill trial recommends a change at least every 3 s.
  • Late cuts. A cut after the word reads as lag. Keep them inside a 0.3 s window.

Source: Andrey Zenin, YyUP_hSovOg at 2:02-2:47. Measurements are ours, accurate to about 0.1 s, from the YouTube file and automatic transcription of a 30 s excerpt the author chose.

title: Technique: a contour spectrum as a voice
label: Shape to sound
summary: Use the magnitudes of a shape's harmonics as the partials of a tone, so the look of a character sets its timbre. All sound is synthesised, so it is deterministic.

blocks.html:
Technique: a contour spectrum as a voice

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The owner's game project synthesises every sound from harmonics: no recordings, no sample packs. Its notes describe one link that suits motion work well: the contour of a character is also its voice. A round character sounds nearly like a sine wave; a spiky one sounds buzzy.

blocks.caption: A circle and a star. Bars: the magnitudes of their first 16 harmonics, normalised. Line: one period of the tone those partials make. The circle is almost one partial; the star spreads over many.

blocks.html:
How it works

A shape is a set of harmonics (harmonic morph). A tone is also a set of harmonics: partials at multiples of one pitch. The project maps one onto the other. For each shape harmonic k it takes the magnitude sqrt(re^2 + im^2), folds the positive and negative frequency together as |k|, ignores the centre term, and uses the result as the level of partial |k|, at most 32 of them, normalised to unit energy. The browser's PeriodicWave builds the waveform from those levels (MDN: PeriodicWave).

Position does not enter, and a uniform change of size only scales all magnitudes, so after normalisation shifting or scaling a character does not change its timbre. Only the silhouette does.

The same notes build short sounds the same way: additive spectra, short amplitude envelopes, pitch sweeps, and percussive texture from three nested sine oscillators instead of random noise. No random number is needed, so the sound is the same on every render.

How to build it

const real = new Float32Array(33), imag = new Float32Array(33);
for (const { k, re, im } of harmonics)
  if (k !== 0 && Math.abs(k) < 33) imag[Math.abs(k)] += Math.hypot(re, im);
const e = Math.hypot(...imag);
for (let k = 1; k < 33; k++) imag[k] /= e;
osc.setPeriodicWave(audioCtx.createPeriodicWave(real, imag));

For a video, render the track offline (OfflineAudioContext) so it is exported as a file, not played live. Then a morph can glide the timbre: recompute the levels from the mixed harmonics at each audio block. We have not tried this part; it follows from the mapping.

Watch for

  • Same shape, same voice. If a mascot changes shape, say whether its voice should change. A fixed identity wants a fixed spectrum.
  • Level. Check loudness numerically, as in render and inspect, and duck under narration.
  • Not a recording. Synthesised tones are clean. Add an envelope (attack, release) or they click.
  • Live audio in a render. A live AudioContext needs a user gesture and follows the wall clock. Do not use it inside a seekable frame pipeline.

Sources: the owner's project notes on harmonic audio (private repository). The demo computes the spectra from real DFTs; we did not render audio.

title: Technique: a storyboard before code, stills before render
label: Storyboard and pre-pass
summary: Show a beat-by-beat storyboard before any code, and render one still per beat before the full render, so problems are found cheaply.

blocks.html:
Technique: a storyboard before code, stills before render

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

The prompts and the tutorial agree on order of work. A prompt ends with the instruction: "First show me the storyboard. Then write the code. After the first render, check 5 frames around every beat and fix the issues before the final render" (flxrnc). Another: "Render one still per beat first. Fix anything cramped, off-grid or hard to read before the full render" (0xnicc0), and "before full render, export one still per major beat (8 frames). Fix cramped type, orphan words, low contrast" (techhalla). In the tutorial, HyperFrames shows a set of key frames before it renders, so feedback comes before it spends 10 minutes and tokens on an MP4 (Mastodon video, 06:04); the author says the key frames were how he saw it was fine and what to correct (07:13).

blocks.caption: Six beat cards with times, then the flow: the storyboard is approved first, code comes second, one still per beat is checked and fixed, and only then the full render.

blocks.html:
How it works

A render is the most expensive way to find a mistake. A storyboard costs a few lines and shows whether the story and the beats are right. A still per beat costs a few seconds each and shows layout problems (cramped type, an orphan word, weak contrast) before the long render. Because a frame is a function of time, stills at the beat times are free to make.

How to build it

  1. Ask for the storyboard as a list of time, what is on screen, what moves for every beat on the beat grid. Approve or edit it.
  2. Write the code. Keep the beats in the timing plan.
  3. Export stills at each beat (and a few frames either side, the prompt says five) and look at them with render and inspect.
  4. Fix what you logged in the error log, then run the full render.

Watch for

  • Skipping step 1 because the idea is simple. A one-line change to the storyboard is cheap; a change to finished code is not.
  • Stills only on the beat. Problems hide between beats; the prompt asks for five frames around each one.
  • Approving the storyboard in prose. Ask for times and counts, not adjectives.

Sources: flxrnc-251921, 0xnicc0-516612, techhalla-498547 in our prompt database, and the ИИ МАСТОДОНТ tutorial yEpN_s9UkAE.

title: Technique: a style contract (style DNA) before any scene
label: Style contract
summary: Turn style words into numbers (line weight, wobble, palette, cadence) and hand them to every scene, so ten shapes look like one set.

blocks.html:
Technique: a style contract

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

"Hand-drawn" is not a style, it is a mood. ProdAdvice's checklist starts with "style DNA" and palettes (10:14). Studio Igor shows the same lesson from the other side: a generic request for pixel art fails, and the second try works because it names a 320 x 180 internal canvas, a sixfold scale and palette cycling (2:32). Later he has the agent write a "style bible" and send it with every image request (17:34).

blocks.caption: Four tokens (line 3 px, redraw 2 px, one blue, 12 drawings a second) applied to a circle, a square and a triangle, against the same three shapes with no contract: each picks its own line weight, wobble and colour.

blocks.html:
How it works

Write the contract as a short list of measurable values and keep it in one file that every scene imports:

  • Paper: background colour and texture.
  • Palette: four or fewer core colours.
  • Line: weight in pixels, and how it varies.
  • Wobble: redraw amplitude and cadence (see Line boil).
  • Shading: hatch angle and spacing (see Hatching).
  • Type and sound: the font, and the character of the sound.

Add two or three approved stills as visual anchors, and describe the mechanisms behind them in words, because a prompt that only says "like this picture" gives you a copy of the picture.

Why numbers

A token can be tested. If the contract says 3 px and a frame shows a 5 px line, that is a defect you can name. "Looks off-style" cannot be fixed by a script or by an assistant that was not in the room.

Watch for

  • Too many tokens. A contract of forty values will not be followed. Keep the ones that change the look.
  • A contract copied from someone else's film. Take the mechanisms (timing, mark types, colour relationships) and make original assets; a reference clip does not give reuse rights.
  • A contract that never changes. When a review finds a better value, update the file and re-render, not just the one scene.

In this studio a new look still goes through the style gate before client use.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 10:14-11:41; Studio Igor, YQ01D9xGAnk at 2:32-3:37 and 17:34-19:12. The token values in the demo are ours.

title: Technique: motion blur from subframes
label: Subframe blur
summary: Draw four samples inside each frame and blend them, so fast movement gets a short streak instead of a sharp hop.

blocks.html:
Technique: motion blur from subframes

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Code-drawn motion is razor sharp: a ball that moves 60 px between frames is two crisp discs, and the eye sees a hop. Two prompts in our database ask for real motion blur and say how: render 4 subframes for each frame (flxrnc); "render 4 subframes per frame, blend (tmix-style)" (techhalla).

blocks.caption: The same ball moving fast. Left: one sample per frame. Right: four samples blended, which leaves a short streak behind the ball.

blocks.html:
How it works
