A camera exposes for a part of the frame time, so a moving object smears. A coded scene can fake this by evaluating the picture at several moments inside one frame and averaging. At 60 fps a frame is 1/60 s; with four subframes the picture is drawn at t, t + 1/4, t + 1/2 and t + 3/4 of that interval and blended into one frame. It works because the picture is a function of time: asking for a time between frames costs nothing.

How to build it

const SUB = 4, FPS = 60;
for (let f = 0; f < frames; f++) {
  clearAccumulator();
  for (let s = 0; s < SUB; s++) {
    renderAt(f / FPS + (s / SUB) / FPS);
    accumulate(canvas, 1 / SUB);     // add this sample with weight 1/4
  }
  writeFrame(accumulator);
}

Rendering is four times slower, so keep it for the final render and test with one sample (render and inspect).

Watch for

  • Blur on text that should be crisp. Fast text can smear into mush; blur the moving layer, not a settled label.
  • Too few subframes on very fast moves. Four samples show visible steps when an object crosses most of the frame in one frame time; add samples or slow the move.
  • Blur and a stable seed. Sample times between frames must not change the seed of a hand-drawn wobble, or the subframes disagree.

Sources: flxrnc-251921, techhalla-498547 in our prompt database. The accumulation loop is ours.

title: Technique: a sharp band that makes a scene look small
label: Tilt-shift band
summary: Blur everything except one horizontal band and a real scene reads as a miniature. Key the band like a camera channel, and seed any grain by frame number.

blocks.html:
Technique: a sharp band that makes a scene look small

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

Miniature faking is an old photographic trick: shoot from above and blur the top and bottom, and the eye reads the scene as a model, because only small things have so shallow a focus (Wikipedia: miniature faking). Our Tabletop Miniature style uses it as its main look: a single post-processing shader does the tilt-shift band and a depth-based blur together, then tone mapping, a colour grade, a vignette and film grain.

blocks.caption: A small town from above, blurred except for one sharp band. The band moves down and rests in the middle. Two copies of the scene: a sharp one, and a blurred one that a mask hides inside the band.

blocks.html:
How it works

The blur size at a pixel (the circle of confusion) is the larger of two values: one from the distance to the band, and one from the scene depth. Inside the band it is zero; outside it grows. The style page uses a 40-tap Vogel-disk gather: for each pixel take 40 samples around it in a spiral, weight each by its own blur size so that sharp objects do not bleed into blurred ones, and sum them.

The band is a number like any other camera value, so it belongs in the same keyed table as the camera curves: move it to the station that matters.

How to build it

The full-screen shader, as a sketch:

float band = smoothstep(uHalf, uHalf + uFall, abs(vUv.y - uCenter));   // 0 in the band, 1 far from it
float coc  = uMaxBlur * max(band, depthCoc);                            // size of the blur disk
for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) {                                          // Vogel disk: golden angle spiral
  float r = sqrt(float(i) + 0.5) / sqrt(40.0), a = float(i) * 2.39996;
  vec2 o = r * coc * vec2(cos(a), sin(a));
  // weight by the sample's own coc, then accumulate colour
}

For a flat scene (no depth buffer) the SVG demo above is enough: a blurred copy and a gradient mask.

Watch for

  • Grain seeded by the wall clock. The style's first version reseeded its grain on a 24 Hz clock, floor(uTime * 24.0). Rendered at 30 fps, that repeats the same grain on one frame in five, so the picture holds still for a frame and then jumps six times a second. It looked like simultaneous white glints on the water. Seed the grain from a frame counter, uFrame = round(t * fps).
  • Measure, do not guess. The diagnosis: group the frame-to-frame change of in-focus blocks by frame index modulo 5. One class sat 46 percent below the others, and about 1 percent after the fix. A six hertz peak in the spectrum of that change was 8.8 times the median before and 1.8 after. Do not answer the symptom by lowering the grain.
  • Soft edges of the band. A hard edge reads as a mask. Give it a gradient.
  • Bokeh and noise from Math.random. The same rule as the grain: derive every random value from the frame number and a seed.
  • Real depth of field is different. The band is a cheat that works from above. Do not use it on an eye-level shot.

Sources: our Tabletop Miniature style page (shader design, the grain pitfall and its measurements); Wikipedia: miniature faking. The GLSL is a sketch of our design, not the style's code; the demo is a 2D imitation.

title: Technique: a timing plan as editable data
label: Timing plan
summary: Write when every object enters, moves and leaves as plain numbers on one timeline, so a late correction is one edit, not a new render of everything.

blocks.html:
Technique: a timing plan as editable data

Motion techniques · Reviewed November 16, 2026

ProdAdvice's central claim is that a coded animation is editable: the assistant writes the graphics and the motion as code, and you change one value. A graphic on screen at 02:50 labels appearance and disappearance times, movement and colour around a common timeline (01:32-03:05). The technique is to write that plan down before any motion exists.

blocks.caption: A 5 s plan as four bars. A playhead sweeps it, then one number changes (the fact label enters at 2.4 s instead of 2.0 s) and only that bar moves; nothing else is redone.

blocks.html:
How it works

Give every object one row with its entrance time, exit time, path, scale or rotation, colour change and layer. In the demo:

Object Plan
Coastline Draws from 0 to 1 s, stays until 4.5 s
Location dot Enters at 1.0 s, stays until 4.5 s
Fact label Enters at 2.0 s (edited to 2.4 s), stays until 4.5 s
Clear Everything leaves from 4.5 s to 5.0 s

The scene reads these numbers; it does not contain them. A missed interval or a wrong coordinate is then fixed in the plan, and you do not regenerate the clip.

How to build it

Keep the plan in one object at the top of the scene file, and let every animation take its start and end from it:

const plan = {
  coast: { in: 0, draw: 1.0, out: 4.5 },
  dot:   { in: 1.0, out: 4.5 },
  fact:  { in: 2.4, out: 4.5 },
  clear: { in: 4.5, out: 5.0 },
};

Build the timeline so it can be sought: the picture at time t depends only on t and the plan, never on what played before. HyperFrames works this way with a single paused timeline (see HyperFrames build rules).

Watch for

  • Numbers hidden inside animations. If a start time lives in a tween, the plan is not the source of truth. Move it out.
  • Timing that ignores the voice. When there is narration, derive the plan from measured word times, not from guesses.
  • A plan with no end state. Always give the last object an exit, or the final frame is whatever was left over.

Source: ProdAdvice, K1Mr5_7Gm3g at 01:32-03:05. The 5 s example is the exercise from HyperFrames tutorial study; the plan format is our proposal.
